extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates / olympiad-style problem solvers in mathematics (students preparing for contest problems and higher-level coursework)
extracted.subtask_description: Hints, heuristics, and pedagogical guidance for solving a broad collection of undergraduate/olympiad-level mathematics problems (algebra, number theory, topology, analysis, algebraic geometry, etc.). Emphasizes methods, common tricks, and learning paths for topics like schemes and algebraic number theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use category theory extensively
rubrics_metrics.description: I use category theory extensively, being a category-lover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author signals a preference for categorical language and tools throughout the notes; expect categorical viewpoints to be used repeatedly when organizing concepts (e.g., chain complexes, functorial arguments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic number theory: 'olympiad spirit' approach
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible I try to keep the algebraic number theory chapter close at heart to an 'olympiad spirit'. Factoring in rings like Z[i] and Z[−5] is very much an olympiad‑flavored topic at heart: one is led naturally to the idea of factoring in general rings of integers, around which the presentation is built.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize concrete, example-driven problems (factoring in specific rings) motivating general theory; use olympiad-style problems as applications (e.g., Chebotarev applied to IMO 2003 Problem 6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three approaches to beginning algebraic geometry / schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three main approaches to beginning the study of schemes: • Only looking at affine and projective varieties, as part of an 'introductory' class, typically an undergraduate course. • Studying affine and projective varieties closely and using them as the motivating example of a scheme, and then developing algebraic geometry from there. • Jumping straight into the definition of a scheme, as in the well-respected and challenging [Va17].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author prefers the second approach (use varieties as motivating examples then introduce schemes), but lists all three as legitimate learning paths; choose approach based on background and taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus first on affine schemes before gluing
rubrics_metrics.description: I made the decision to, at least for the second part, focus mostly on affine schemes. These already generalize varieties in several ways, and I think the jump is too much if one starts then gluing schemes together. I would rather that the student first feel like they really understand how an affine scheme works, before going on into the world where they now have a general scheme X which is locally affine (but probably not itself affine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedagogical standard: master affine schemes thoroughly via many examples before introducing general schemes and gluing constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommend concrete references for further study
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred introductory and advanced references are signalled throughout: e.g., [Og10], [Le02] for algebraic number theory (Chebotarev), [Ga03] and [Va17] for algebraic geometry, [Mi95] for Riemann surfaces, [Hi13] for analytic number theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these recommended notes/books for deeper reading; author notes relative strengths (e.g., [Ga03] for first read, [Va17] for serious version).

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch the long exact sequence in action for short exact sequences of chain complexes
rubrics_metrics.description: 0 → A• → B• → C• → 0 is a short exact sequence of chain complexes. Write out the corresponding long exact sequence. Nearly all terms will vanish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the long exact sequence of homology/cohomology associated to a short exact sequence of chain complexes to deduce vanishing or compute groups; analyze which terms vanish to simplify conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use orders to analyze group homomorphisms and isomorphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Several hints advise 'look at orders' or 'consider orders' when determining maps or counting possibilities (e.g., 1C, 1G, 3D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard technique: compare element orders, use properties of prime orders, and pick generators by order to construct/identify subgroups and homomorphisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply Fermat's little theorem / elementary number theory lemmas
rubrics_metrics.description: Hints like 'Copy the proof of Fermat’s little theorem, using Lemma 1.2.5' occur frequently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appropriate reduce to known elementary number theory lemmas (Fermat/Euler) and apply them directly or copy standard proofs adapted to the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rank–nullity and dimension arguments in linear algebra
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the rank-nullity theorem and dimension-counting strategies to show injectivity/surjectivity relations and analyze kernels/images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical approach: compute dimensions of kernel and image, use stabilization of chains of subspaces (for powers of linear maps), and apply to deduce structure (e.g., eventual stabilization implies properties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pick a convenient basis (or eigenbasis) to simplify linear-algebra problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Many solutions begin 'take a basis' or 'write T in an eigenbasis', e.g., to diagonalize linear maps or compute determinants/traces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly choose bases (orthonormal, Jordan, eigenbasis) to reduce linear operators/matrices to simple forms and make calculations or structural arguments immediate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Cayley–Hamilton, diagonalization, or Jordan form where useful
rubrics_metrics.description: Hints mention Cayley–Hamilton and diagonalization as tools to solve matrix/linear algebra problems (e.g., invertibility, eigenvalue arguments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When direct manipulations are messy, apply Cayley–Hamilton or choose a diagonal/Jordan form to simplify algebraic relationships among matrices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider chains ker T ⊆ ker T^2 ⊆ ... and im T ⊇ im T^2 ⊇ ... to argue stabilization
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the fact that these chains must eventually stabilize (for dimension reasons) to derive conclusions about nilpotency, ranks, or other properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dimension/stabilization arguments can show eventual constancy leading to structural conclusions (e.g., on generalized eigenspaces).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Pigeonhole Principle and combinatorial double-counting
rubrics_metrics.description: Hints repeatedly advise pigeonhole or double-counting (e.g., 16C 'Double-count pairs (g,x) with g·x = x') and other elementary combinatorial arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard counting/combinatorial tools: orbit-stabilizer, double-counting, pigeonhole, often combined with group action reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Burnside’s lemma and orbit–stabilizer for counting orbits
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply Burnside's lemma directly to count colorings/configurations and use the orbit-stabilizer theorem to analyze orbit sizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When counting up-to-symmetry, compute fixed-point counts and average, or use orbit-stabilizer divisibility properties to restrict possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Baire category arguments for topological existence-type results
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard solution for some problems is via the so-called 'Baire category theorem'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For existence or genericity in complete metric spaces, consider Baire category as a tool to show nonempty intersections of dense open sets or to construct points with desired properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct Cauchy sequences / completion for metric completion problems
rubrics_metrics.description: To construct completions, let M be the set of Cauchy sequences modulo relation that limit distances go to zero; use this quotient to form the completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly build completion via equivalence classes of Cauchy sequences and use limit properties to define the metric and verify completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-compactness via diagonal subsequence argument
rubrics_metrics.description: For X×Y compactness: given sequence (pi) in X×Y, take a subsequence so x-coordinates converge, then a subsequence of that so y-coordinates converge; the resulting subsequence converges in product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do sequential compactness proof by passing to subsequences iteratively (diagonal argument); beware of mistakenly treating independent subsequences as linked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contrapositive metric construction to prove non-compactness implies existence of unbounded homeomorphic metric
rubrics_metrics.description: If M is not compact, construct an unbounded continuous function F:M→R and define d'(x,y):=d(x,y)+|F(x)−F(y)| to get an unbounded metric homeomorphic to the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct explicit continuous functions from the space to R to modify the metric and force/unmask desired properties; standard trick in topology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use continuity definitions appropriately (sequential vs open-set)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two approaches to show 'no continuous injective map from Q to N': metric/sequential reasoning or open-set topology argument noting singletons are not open in Q but are open in N.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the more natural definition of continuity for the setting: sequential arguments often suffice in metric contexts; open-set arguments are cleaner topologically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Taylor series and complex-analytic uniqueness principles
rubrics_metrics.description: To show uniqueness or analytic continuation-type results, look at Taylor series coefficients and apply Cauchy differentiation formula (e.g., zeros accumulating implies function is zero).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use power-series expansions and analytic continuation/identity theorems: if zeros accumulate, coefficients vanish forcing identically zero functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contour integration tricks: ML-lemma, wedge contours, semicircles
rubrics_metrics.description: For complex integrals use ML-estimation, wedge contours, sectors of circles, and semicircle arguments to evaluate improper integrals or show integrals vanish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard complex-analysis contour integration approaches include constructing appropriate contours and using ML-estimate to bound integrals over arcs as radius→∞.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply Parseval / Fourier series for function integral/series problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Parseval's identity for Fourier coefficients to compute integrals like ∫ x^2 or expected values of Boolean functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parseval connects L^2 norms with Fourier coefficients; apply it when orthogonality or energy-methods are applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use structure theorems for modules / finitely generated abelian groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the structure theorem (e.g., decomposition into cyclic modules or invariant factors) to analyze modules or abelian groups; use over k[x] when algebraically closed simplifications apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce problems about finitely generated modules to canonical decomposition forms and analyze blocks/factors separately; use specialization if the base ring is algebraically closed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use norms and traces in algebraic number theory arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: The norm is multiplicative and equals the product of Galois conjugates; traces and norms are used to show integrality/divisibility properties in rings of integers and to relate ideals and residues (e.g., showing elements of OK satisfy divisibility by p).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute norms/traces to detect divisibility, to show elements lie in subrings, or to relate ideals to finite quotients; common in proofs about primes, class groups, and unit arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Minkowski’s theorem (geometry of numbers) for ideal/class group arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Mimic proofs of Minkowski-type statements when constructing ideals or showing existence of elements (e.g., constructing small norm elements in given ideals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Minkowski convex-body arguments when you need existence of nontrivial elements in lattices or bounds on ideal norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor problems into simpler algebraic or modular reductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many arithmetic hints say 'work mod p', 'clear denominators', 'factor in Q(i)' etc.—standard tactic: reduce or factor in an appropriate ring to simplify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a modulus or extension where the algebra simplifies (e.g., finite fields, cyclotomic fields, Gaussian integers) to get control over solutions or structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use homotopy / homology tools: pick appropriate subspaces and apply exact sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Topological problems: reduce to homotopy equivalence (e.g., R^n	o S^{n−1}), use relative homology, or find short exact sequences of chain complexes to apply long exact sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate geometric/topological questions into computations on homology/cohomology; choose Mayer–Vietoris or long exact sequences after cutting into convenient pieces.
